headline: Skyroot orbits. NASA aborts. SpaceX stalls.
deck: This week saw mixed results in space launches and funding, with some projects gaining altitude while others face delays.

stories.head: Skyroot Aerospace hits orbit; now what?
stories.body: Skyroot Aerospace successfully launched its Vikram-1 rocket into orbit, marking a significant milestone for Indian commercial space efforts. This comes as the company aims to capitalize on a burgeoning market, though the real test will be sustaining momentum beyond this initial success. The launch has potential implications for India's position in the global space race, where reliability can be more valuable than speed.
stories.soWhat: Skyroot's success is a reminder that in aerospace, the first flight is just the beginning; maintaining the trajectory is the real challenge.

stories.head: NASA cancels Draper lunar lander mission.
stories.body: In a move that surprised few, NASA has terminated the Draper lunar lander mission, citing development delays. This decision underscores the agency's ongoing struggle with project management, a recurring theme in large-scale aerospace endeavors. The cancellation comes as NASA shifts its focus to other lunar initiatives, potentially reallocating resources to more promising projects.
stories.soWhat: This termination illustrates that even the most ambitious plans can fall victim to the realities of execution; NASA's budget is finite, and every misstep is costly.

stories.head: True Anomaly raises $190M; defense pulls through.
stories.body: True Anomaly secured $190 million in Series C funding, bringing its valuation to $1.6 billion as it focuses on co-orbital security and space domain awareness. This round highlights the increasing interest from the Department of Defense in private sector capabilities, as True Anomaly positions itself as a key player in national security. The funding reflects a broader trend of defense agencies looking to leverage commercial innovation.
stories.soWhat: True Anomaly's success is a sign that in the current climate, cash is king, especially when it comes with a DoD stamp of approval.

watchlist.title: SpaceX's Starship delays continue.
watchlist.body: With another launch attempt aborted, investors will be watching closely to see if SpaceX can regain its momentum or if this becomes a pattern.

watchlist.title: Palantir's TITAN extension implications.
watchlist.body: The $480 million extension for the TITAN program may signal increased government reliance on data analytics in defense, which could open doors for more contracts.

watchlist.title: Sierra Space's Dream Chaser progress.
watchlist.body: Having cleared its critical design review, the Dream Chaser's next steps will be closely monitored as it aims for a timely launch amid a crowded field.

watchlist.title: Artemis Accords expansion.
watchlist.body: Serbia's signing of the Artemis Accords may lead to more countries aligning with U.S. lunar ambitions, complicating the geopolitical landscape.

talent.statLabel: Job orders YoY · plus 2 starters per head, an 8-year first
talent.head: Demand has doubled. So has our hit rate.
talent.body: EVONA's job orders are up 2.0× year-over-year, and for the first time in our eight-year history we're placing two new starters per EVONA staff member. The first number says demand is real. The second says we're converting it, which in recruitment is the only number that actually matters. Growth is heaviest in Series B/C startups; primes are running flat. Compensation isn't the variable. The constraint is schedule risk in the primes: senior engineers leave Boeing, Lockheed, Northrop because they want to ship hardware before retirement.

Palantir's stock remains buoyed by its defense contracts, but analysts are questioning long-term growth prospects.
